MAINE BLACK CHAMBER OF COMMERCE
mainebcc.com
Submitted by: Joshua Brister (President) Maine Black Chamber of Commerce (MBCC) Re: LD 2107 -- An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program Position: Opposed

January, 29th 2026

Good Morning Chair and Members of the Committee,

On behalf of the Maine Black Chamber of Commerce (MBCC), I respectfully submit this testimony in opposition to LD 2107 -- An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program. While MBCC appreciates the intent to promote safety for nonprofit organizations, we are deeply concerned that this bill, as currently written, fails to define equitable criteria for resource allocation, and does not adequately address the very real threats faced by Black American business owners in Maine.

Many Black businesses in Maine encounter heightened risk related to prejudice, discrimination, and bias, yet the general language of this proposal does not prioritize resources for that community most affected by hate, harassment, and racially motivated threats. In today's racial climate, where the fallout from biased actions can directly suppress economic participation, it is critical that any security grant program explicitly centers business owners and not NPO's. Without this clarity, well-intentioned programs risk distributing funds in ways that are not responsive to the lived experiences of the overall Black business community.

Furthermore, MBCC is concerned that LD 2107 lacks sufficient guardrails to prevent waste, fraud, and abuse that commonly emerges in loosely defined grant programs, particularly when oversight mechanisms and accountability standards are not clearly articulated. Maine has seen too many instances where broad grant funds are spent with little transparency or meaningful impact reporting, disproportionately disadvantaging small Black American businesses.

Until these concerns are addressed, MBCC cannot support LD 2107, as it currently stands.

Sincerely,
Joshua Brister
President Maine Black Chamber of Commerce

Testimony of Marpheen Chann for Khmer Maine before the Joint Standing Committee on the Judiciary
IN SUPPORT OF L.D. 2107 An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program
On January 29th, 2026
Senator Carney, Representative Moonen, and distinguished members of the Judiciary Committee:
My name is Marpheen Chann, and I am the Executive Director of Khmer Maine, a community organization that serves Maine's Cambodian and Southeast Asian communities, of which there are more than 10,000 who call Maine home.
I am here today because the older generation in our community came to this country to escape violence. They survived the Khmer Rouge. They rebuilt their lives here in Maine. They established temples and community spaces where they could practice their faith and culture in peace. They should not have to fear violence again.
This is not just a problem for other states. Right here in Maine, our Jewish neighbors have received specific violent death threats. Our Muslim neighbors fear coming to mosque for daily prayers. Buddhist temples have experienced break-ins and hateful messages. More than 20 states have already created nonprofit security grant programs to help communities protect themselves. Maine should join them.
L.D. 2107 would create a $2 million grant program administered by the Attorney General's Office to help religious institutions and nonprofits improve their security. This includes physical security upgrades, security personnel, and other measures to protect against hate crimes and terror attacks.
This bill is about more than buildings. It is about people. Our elders who want to pray in peace. Parents who want to bring their children to religious services without fear. Community members who gather to celebrate holidays and milestones. They deserve to feel safe.
I urge this committee to support L.D. 2107. Our communities should not have to choose between practicing their faith and fearing for their safety.
Thank you for your time and consideration.
Sincerely,
Marpheen Chann Executive Director, Khmer Maine Portland, Maine
10059106:
Dear Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and members of Judiciary Committee,
My name is Mary Alice Scott, and I am the Public Affairs Manager at Maine Association of Nonprofits (MANP). MANP is a growing membership organization made up of over 1,000 nonprofit members from all 16 counties. For 30 years, MANP has grown to become Maine's comprehensive resource for the tools, knowledge, and connections nonprofits need to be effective and well-run.
We are submitting testimony Neither For Nor Against LD 2107: An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program.
Nonprofits are community-based organizations that serve a charitable purpose. Nonprofits are an important part of civil society. They are often set up to provide a way to channel collective efforts towards social good. They can be shelters for victims of domestic violence, social services for people who are homeless, care for those with mental illness, assistance for immigrant resettlement, group homes, and residential treatment for drug addiction. They can also be a faith-based organization, a community theater, museum, dance troupe, an outdoors group, a youth athletic club, and so on. They all have the right to associate to express their beliefs through their work and activities without fear of security threats or violence.
Nonprofits have experienced property damage, vandalism, graffiti, theft, security breaches and even violent threats because of their missions, or, in the case of faithbased organizations, because of their faith.
This type of grant program is being passed in many other states, including Rhode Island, and there is obviously a need. MANP recognizes that need, and yet we also recognize that there are many other communities and types of organizations that are impacted by hate crimes or the threat of terror attacks. We would urge the committee to support the intent of the bill while ensuring that communities across the state are similarly protected by hate crimes and terror attacks.
When it is time for administrative implementation of the program, we would be happy to give input to the appropriate office about what may be useful when it comes to selection criteria and/or other ways to ensure the appropriations are transparent and beneficial.
Thank you for your time and consideration.

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn and distinguished members of the Joint Standing Committee on
Judiciary, my name is Michael Brennan, and I represent House District 115, which is part of Portland.
Thank you for the oppoitunity to present LD 2107, An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit
Security Grant Program.
In recent years, our country has seen far too many violent attacks against community gatherings -- hate crimes against groups of innocent people based on their faith traditions, who they love, where they were born or the color of their skin. Even so, few non-profit organizations have the resources to pay for necessary protective measures. This bill is about making sure non-profits have the tools to keep people
safe and secure from acts of terrorism and extremism.
A number of states have established grant programs to help non-profit organizations implement
security measures, including reinforced doors, access control systems, security persomiel and more.
Maine should act now to join those states by passing LD 2107.
You will hear fromlcommunity leaders today about the risks they are facing and how this measure will help protect the people they serve. Before I tum it over to them, I would like to offer two modest
amendments to the bill for the committee's consideration.
First, I suggest the grant program should be administered by the Maine Emergency Management
Agency (MEMA) instead of the Attorney General's Office as specified in the original bill. In previous
years, MEMA has administered a similar grant program funded by the federal government, but the future of that federal program is in doubt. Because MEMA has been doing this work, I believe it is in
the best position to continue it without interruption.
Second, I suggest reducing the appropriation from $2 million to $1.5 million. I believe this level of
funding is appropriate when compared to the funding that other, larger states have dedicated to similar
programs.
Thank you for your consideration. I would be happy to answer any questions you may have for me.

Dear Chair Carney, Chair Kuhn, and Members of the Judiciary Committee,
On behalf of ADL (the Anti-Defamation League) New England, I am pleased to submit this testimony in support of LD 2107, "An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program." I urge the Committee to support LD 2107, which would create a security grant program in the Office of the Attorney General to provide grants to assist nonprofit organizations to improve security needs at their establishments to protect against hate crimes and terror attacks. This is an important step towards achieving safety and security for all who are at a high-risk of targeted hate.
As the leading anti-hate organization in the world, founded in 1913, ADL's mission is "to stop the defamation of the Jewish people and to secure justice and fair treatment for all." We are a world leader in countering hatred, bigotry, and bias in all forms, and we have organizational expertise and knowledge around the need to protect vulnerable communities.
Authorizing $2 million for the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program will support critical security measures at faith-based and other nonprofit community institutions. At a time of heightened antisemitic incidents across Maine, these funds are critical to safeguarding our communities and preventing further acts of antisemitism.
Maine has experienced a troubling rise of hateful graffiti on synagogues, bomb threats to religious institutions, and hate mail sent to faith-based centers. According to ADL data, Maine saw antisemitic incidents increase dramatically from 13 incidents in 2022 to 53 in 2023--a more than 300% increase-- with incidents remaining elevated at 51 in 2024. This alarming trend underscores the urgent need for enhanced security measures to protect Jewish communities.
The Nonprofit Security Grant Program would provide funding for targeted institutions to take the necessary precautions and security measures to keep their communities safe from extremist threats. These grants would allow organizations to make physical security enhancements, cover the costs of security personnel, and develop safety plans and protocols to ensure that everyone in Maine can feel safe when they worship, study, and spend time in communal spaces. By passing LD 2107 with funding for the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, Maine will be taking a critical step towards protecting its residents amidst an alarming rise in antisemitic and other hate incidents across the state.
Thank you for your consideration,
Samantha Joseph
Regional Director
ADL New England

My name is Scott Nussinow, and I am a resident of Auburn. I am also a longtime member of Temple Shalom in Auburn, a member of its Board of Directors, and Chair of its Safety and Security Committee. I am writing to express my strong support for LD 2107.

However, over the past year, FEMA reimbursement delays, with no explanation or timeline for payment, have severely constrained our ability to proceed responsibly. As a small congregation with a modest and carefully managed budget, we simply cannot cash-flow these expenses. I respectfully urge your support for LD 2107 and thank you for your consideration of this important legislation.
Sincerely,

Testimony of Suzanne Lafreniere, on behalf of the Catholic Diocese LD 2107 An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program
Senator Carney and Representative Kuhn and all members of the Joint Standing Committee on Judiciary, my name is Suzanne Lafreniere and I represent the Roman Catholic Diocese of Portland in its support of LD 2107, An Act to Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program. The diocese presently has a population of 279,159 Catholics. In addition to its 48 parishes, it has eight elementary schools, one private elementary/middle school, and one private high school. It also includes one Catholic college, Saint Joseph's College of Maine in Standish. Within the diocese, there are also seven subsidized housing units, four rehabilitation and residence facilities, and two child-care centers. There are three Catholic hospitals operating independently of the diocese as well as Catholic Charities Maine, the state's largest social service agency, which operates as a separate corporation.
Our diocese encompasses parishes, missions, schools, and charitable ministries serving communities from our coastal towns to our most rural areas. Each parish campus is more than a building; it is a spiritual home, a gathering place, and often a key provider of food assistance, crisis support, and community programs for our neighbors regardless of faith background. In a time of increasing polarization, religious communities and other nonprofits are facing a heightened risk of harassment, vandalism, and, in some cases, violence. We have a moral responsibility to protect the people who walk through our doors--children, the elderly, volunteers, and staff--so they can worship, learn, and serve in safety.
LD 2107 takes a prudent, targeted approach to this responsibility. The bill would establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program in the Office of the Attorney General to provide grants to nonprofit organizations to "improve security at property owned or occupied by those nonprofit organizations to protect against hate crimes and terror attacks." It authorizes support for three essential categories: physical security enhancements, the cost of security personnel, and the development or enhancement of security plans and protocols. These are precisely the tools that allow organizations like ours to move from good intentions to concrete, professional, and effective safety measures.
For Catholic parishes and schools, this program could mean installing secure entry systems at buildings that currently have open, easily accessible doors; improving exterior lighting in rural parking lots where evening Masses, youth ministry, or recovery meetings take place; updating camera systems that are outdated or nonexistent; and ensuring that staff and volunteers have clear, trained protocols for responding to an emergency. It could also allow us to conduct formal security assessments and develop written security plans that align with best practices and with federal programs such as the Nonprofit Security Grant Program, ensuring that state investments are coordinated and efficient rather than duplicative.

There has been a sustained pattern of vandalism, arson, and threats against Catholic churches and related sites across the United States since 2020, with several hundred incidents documented by Catholic and church-monitoring organizations. Overall scale
� A Catholic advocacy group has tracked more than 500 alleged attacks on Catholic churches in the U.S. since late May 2020, including arson, smashed windows, destroyed statues, and graffiti.1
� The U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops has separately logged at least 400-plus publicly reported incidents of arson, vandalism, or other destruction at Catholic sites across 43 states and Washington, D.C. in roughly the same period.2
This program is also structured in a way that respects the diversity of Maine's nonprofit sector. It does not privilege one faith or mission; it is open to nonprofit organizations broadly, including houses of worship, schools, community centers, and social service providers. That breadth is important to us as a Catholic diocese. Our concern is not only for our own churches but also for synagogues, mosques, temples, and secular nonprofits that share our commitment to the dignity of every human person and that may be targeted because of who they are or whom they serve. LD 2107 provides a framework for the State to partner with this entire ecosystem to reduce the risk of catastrophic harm.
In Catholic social teaching, government has a legitimate role in promoting the common good and protecting the vulnerable. LD 2107 is an expression of that role. It does not fund religious activities, doctrine, or worship. Rather, it helps ensure that Mainers of all faiths and none can gather, receive services, and contribute to civic life without undue fear for their safety. It is a measured investment in prevention that is far less costly--in human and financial terms--than responding after a tragedy.
For these reasons, on behalf of the Diocese of Portland, I respectfully urge you to vote Ought to Pass on LD 2107. Thank you for your attention and for your service to the people of Maine. I would be happy to answer any questions.

Holocaust and Human Rights Center of Maine Augusta, Maine January 28, 2026
Dear Chair Carney and distinguished members of the Judiciary Committee,
On behalf of the Holocaust and Human Rights Center of Maine (HHRC), I am writing to express our strong support for LD 2107, An Act To Establish the Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program.
HHRC works statewide to advance human rights education, combat antisemitism and other forms of hate, and support communities that are too often the targets of bias-motivated harassment and violence. Our programs regularly engage Jewish communities, immigrant and refugee communities, students, educators, libraries, and civic spaces that are open to the public and committed to democratic values. Unfortunately, these are also the very spaces that increasingly face real and documented security threats.
Across Maine, nonprofit organizations serving marginalized or historically targeted populations are contending with rising incidents of hate, intimidation, and threats. Jewish institutions, Muslim communities, LGBTQ+ organizations, restorative and social justice groups, and human rights organizations alike have had to divert scarce programmatic resources toward basic safety measures--often without access to dedicated funding or technical guidance. This reality undermines the collective ability to carry out missions and places both staff and participants at risk.
LD 2107 represents a proactive, responsible, and values-aligned response. By establishing a Maine Nonprofit Security Grant Program, the Legislature would help ensure that nonprofits can take reasonable, preventative steps to protect their facilities, staff, and the public without compromising their openness or educational missions. Security enhancements such as cameras, lighting, access controls, and emergency planning are not luxuries; they are now essential infrastructure for many organizations doing public-facing work.
Importantly, this bill affirms that safety and inclusion are not competing priorities. When nonprofits are supported in creating secure environments, they are better able to foster dialogue, education, and community connection, core pillars of a healthy democracy. Preventative investment in security also reduces the likelihood of more costly and traumatic outcomes later, benefiting both communities and the state as a whole.
For HHRC, LD 2107 aligns directly with our commitment to dignity, accountability, and the protection of civil society. Ensuring that nonprofits can operate safely sends a clear message that Maine stands with those working to uphold human rights and reject hate in all its forms. We respectfully urge the Legislature to support LD 2107 and to recognize nonprofit security as a shared public responsibility.
Thank you for your leadership and consideration of this important measure.
Sincerely,
Tam Huynh Executive Director of the Holocaust and Human Rights Center of Maine

Senator Carney, Representative Kuhn, and Esteemed Members of the Committee:
My name is Zach Schwartz. I live in Westbrook, Maine, and I am testifying in strong support of LD 2107, An Act to Establish the Maine Nonpro t Security Grant Program. Thank you for your time and consideration.
Over the last few years, Jewish organizations across Maine and the US have faced the highest levels of antisemitism seen since the Holocaust. In 2025, multiple Jewish institutions in Maine received speci c death threats, letters saying things like "I will kill all at this place." Flyers urging people to enact a "DDay" against the Jewish community were posted in Portland. Another yer in Bethel stated that Jews were no longer welcome in Maine. In a recent survey of Maine Jewish adults, 52% said they avoided activities in the past year out of fear of antisemitism, and 35% reported experiencing antisemitic remarks, vandalism, or threats.
This bill grew directly out of what I heard while visiting synagogues across the state: "We're facing the highest threat levels we've ever seen, and we're running out of security funds." These synagogues should not have to choose between keeping their doors open and keeping people safe.
However, this is not just a Jewish community issue. As I have spoken with other partners--churches, mosques, Buddhist temples, and nonpro ts serving a variety of causes--I heard the same concerns about rising threats, safety, and preparedness. In 2025, there were multiple violent attacks on Catholic organizations, Mormon organizations, Jewish organizations, and many others in the United States.
I'm here today representing over 20 organizations that have signed an open letter supporting this legislation--this letter includes the majority of Maine's Jewish institutions, a historic black church in the Green Memorial AME Zion Church, the state's largest Buddhist Temple Watt Samaki, a Southern Maine mosque, and nonpro ts and houses of worship across Maine.
LD 2107 is a unity bill. Similar nonpro t security grant programs have passed in at least 18 other states, oftentimes with strong bipartisan support. This bill's support is not along geographic lines--while many nonpro ts and houses of worship reside in the state's cities, there are many rural churches in towns which don't have professional police departments, or for whom it would take 15, 20, 30 minutes for law enforcement to arrive. And this bill's support should not be along political lines--while there is strong Democrat support for this bill, the horri c murder of Charlie Kirk last year shows us that organizations and people with conservative values are also being targeted. This is a bill for all of us.
Some may ask: "Isn't there federal nonpro t security funding?" There is, and it helps--but it is highly competitive and often reimburses after costs are incurred, which many small organizations cannot front. Additionally, the federal program does not cover public security personnel, which many synagogues and houses of worship have urged me is the single most effective and important measure they can take to feel safe.
LD 2107 is a modest, commonsense, unifying bill that can prevent tragedy. As much as it pains me to say, it is not "if" a next attack against a house of worship or nonpro t happens, it is "when." And I hope that if and when--G-d forbid--that moment should come, we can say that we did all we could to ensure houses of worships and nonpro ts were ready and safe.
I respectfully urge you to support LD 2107 and report it out Ought to Pass. Thank you.
